name: Glyndebourne
funding: Charity. Of £43.4M income in 2025, 48% was box office and £10.3M fundraising and memberships; Arts Council England gave £0.8M for the Autumn Season (2025 accounts).
watch: MPs and peers declared Glyndebourne tickets and hospitality from Japan Tobacco International between 2011 and 2014 (Register of Members' Financial Interests via Tobacco Tactics).

overview: John Christie and his wife, the soprano Audrey Mildmay, opened an opera theatre at Glyndebourne, a country house near Lewes, and the first season began on 28 May 1934 with Le nozze di Figaro (Wikipedia).
The present theatre, designed by Michael and Patty Hopkins, seats about 1,200 and opened on 28 May 1994; it cost £34 million, 90% of it from donations (Wikipedia).

It is run by Glyndebourne Productions Ltd, a company limited by guarantee and registered charity (number 243877) incorporated in 1939; Gus Christie, grandson of the founder, is Executive Chairman and Stephen Langridge Artistic Director (2025 accounts).
In 2025 it reached a live audience of over 130,000 across 107 mainstage opera and concert performances, filling 99% of seats (2025 accounts).
A wind turbine on the estate began operating in January 2012, and its electricity sales go through the trading subsidiary Glyndebourne Enterprises Ltd (Wikipedia; 2024 accounts).
details.funding_verdict: Glyndebourne: box office, members and donors, with a small Arts Council grant
funding: Total income was £43.4 million in 2025 (2024: £41.9 million); 48% came from box office and £10.3 million (24%) from fundraising and memberships (2025 accounts).
Box office income in 2025 was £20.741 million, memberships £2.679 million, donations £3.478 million and legacies £1.404 million in unrestricted funds (2025 accounts).
Government sources in 2025 were Theatre Tax Relief of £3.7 million and an Arts Council England grant of £812,800 for the Autumn Season and Learning and Engagement programme (2025 accounts).
The accounts state that the Festival receives no public subsidy and relies on fundraising and box office (2024 accounts).

Arts Council England cut its grant by 52% for 2023-26, which led Glyndebourne to cancel its 2023 Tour after more than 50 years of touring and start an Autumn Season at Glyndebourne instead (2023 accounts).
Sponsorship of productions released to income was £960,000 in 2025 and £635,000 in 2024, alongside Glyndebourne Festival Society fees of £2.131 million (2025 and 2024 accounts).
The corporate partners page names Bolney, Morgan Motor Company, English Woodlands, French Bedroom, Lanson Champagne and WILDSMITH (Glyndebourne website).
Reserves are invested mainly with Capital Group (£46.0 million) and Rothschild (£1.7 million) at 31 December 2024 (2024 accounts).
wider_context: Japan Tobacco International hosted MPs and peers at Glyndebourne: Brian Binley declared two tickets worth £1,132.80 in 2011, Gerald Kaufman two tickets and hospitality worth about £1,278 in 2013, and Lord Trimble and Baroness Wheatcroft were guests of JTI on 24 July 2014 (Registers of Interests via Tobacco Tactics).

A blog post of 15 December 2011 said the 2009 Glyndebourne Festival annual report listed JTI among corporate supporters; that report was not available to check, and JTI is not named on Glyndebourne's current partners page (An Overgrown Path; Glyndebourne website).

case_notes.title: Register of Members' Financial Interests
case_notes.text: The Register of Members' Financial Interests records Japan Tobacco International giving seven MPs tickets and hospitality at Glyndebourne: Brian Binley in May 2011 (£1,132.80); Christopher Chope, Jim Dowd, Gerald Kaufman and Robert Walter on 13 June 2013 (£1,278 to £1,534 each); and Nick Brown and a guest in July 2014, with Glyndebourne named as co-donor.

grade_basis: No flagged funder or funding protest on record, and the amounts are given.

name: Brisbane Festival
funding: Queensland Government and Brisbane City Council are foundation partners; the state gave $5.29M a year through Arts Queensland in 2012-13. Platinum partners include Australian Retirement Trust (festival website).
watch: Santos GLNG backed the festival's City of Lights laser show in 2012 and 2013; the festival's partnerships page quotes casino operator The Star Entertainment Group.
why_flagged: The Queensland ministerial diary records the Arts Minister at the opening of Santos GLNG City of Lights in conjunction with Brisbane Festival on 7 September 2013, and the festival's partnerships page, retrieved 17 November 2026, carries a partner quote from The Star Entertainment Group, a casino operator (Wikipedia).

overview: Brisbane Festival began in 1996 as a joint initiative of the Queensland Government and Brisbane City Council, succeeding the Warana Festival first held in 1962; it became annual in 2009 when it merged with Riverfire (Wikipedia).
It runs for about three weeks each September, and artistic directors have included Tony Gould, Lyndon Terracini, Noel Staunton, David Berthold and Louise Bezzina (Wikipedia).

The 2025 festival was expected to draw about 1.8 million locals and visitors to 1,069 performances by more than 2,200 artists, nearly half of the 106 productions free (Queensland Government, 5 September 2025).
Its head office is at Level 2, 381 Brunswick Street, Fortitude Valley (festival website).
details.funding_verdict: Brisbane Festival: state and city government with corporate partners
funding: The Queensland Government and Brisbane City Council are named as Foundation Partners on the festival's partnerships page (festival website).

The Queensland Government invested $5.29 million in Brisbane Festival through Arts Queensland in 2012, and Arts Queensland's annual investment was given as $5.29 million in 2013 (Queensland Government, 8 September 2012; Dance Informa, 17 April 2013).
The state provides annual operational funding, and gave a further $178,850 for a capacity building program in 2023 (Queensland Government, 30 June 2023).

Platinum Partners on the current partnerships page, using 2025 logos, are Australian Retirement Trust, Southbank and Verso Projects; Airbnb, CPL, QIC and The University of Queensland hold named partner roles, and ANZ and QPAC are Major Partners (festival website).
Riverfire, the festival's fireworks night, is presented by Australian Retirement Trust (Queensland Government, 5 September 2025).
The partnerships page carries a partner testimonial attributed to The Star Entertainment Group beside a picture of Queen's Wharf (festival website).

Santos GLNG Project and Tourism and Events Queensland supported City of Lights, the laser show that opened the 2013 festival and drew more than 300,000 spectators in 2012 (Dance Informa, 17 April 2013); the 2012 Arts Minister's statement lists Santos GLNG City of Lights among the festival's events (Queensland Government, 8 September 2012).

red_flags.heading: Fossil fuel sponsorship
points: The Arts Minister, Ian Walker, attended the opening night function of Santos GLNG City of Lights in conjunction with Brisbane Festival on 7 September 2013 as a guest of the festival (Queensland Government ministerial diary, September 2013).
GLNG produces coal seam gas from the Surat and Bowen basins and liquefies it on Curtis Island near Gladstone; Santos is its operator with a 30% stake (Wikipedia).

red_flags.heading: Gambling
points: The Star Entertainment Group operates casinos including The Star Sydney and The Star Gold Coast, and in 2022 regulators found it unsuitable to hold its New South Wales and Queensland casino licences (Wikipedia).
The Star Brisbane timed its phased opening at Queen's Wharf for 29 August 2024 to coincide with Brisbane Festival (InDaily, Bonnie Liston, 1 July 2024).

case_notes.title: Queensland ministerial diaries
case_notes.text: Queensland ministerial diaries record the Arts Minister, Ian Walker, at the opening night function of the Santos GLNG City of Lights with Brisbane Festival on 7 September 2013, and the Tourism Minister, Jann Stuckey, at the Santos GLNG City of Lights show with Tourism and Events Queensland and Brisbane Festival on 25 September 2013.

grade_basis: Funders tied to fossil fuels and gambling.

name: State Library of Queensland
funding: Queensland Government statutory body. Of $101.8M income in 2025-26, $77.1M was an administered state grant; donations and sponsorships were $1.5M (2025-26 annual report).
watch: Arrow Energy, the Shell and PetroChina coal seam gas joint venture, funded State Library literacy programs in the Western Downs from December 2013.
why_flagged: The Arts Minister spoke at the State Library/Arrow Energy partnership launch on 4 December 2013 (Queensland ministerial diary, December 2013); Arrow is owned 50:50 by Shell and PetroChina (ACCC, 13 April 2010).

overview: The library began in 1896 as the Brisbane Public Library, was renamed the Public Library of Queensland in 1898 and moved to its South Bank site in 1988; the John Oxley Library, a research centre for Queensland material, opened in 1934 (Wikipedia).
A 2004 to 2006 redevelopment by Donovan Hill and Peddle Thorp enlarged the building, which reopened in November 2006 (Wikipedia).

It is governed by the Library Board of Queensland, a Queensland Government statutory body under the Libraries Act 1988, and its controlled entity Queensland Library Foundation raises funds for it (Wikipedia; 2025-26 annual report).

It recorded 1.8 million onsite visits and 5.6 million online sessions in 2025-26, and administered $32.7 million in public library and First 5 Forever funding on behalf of the state (2025-26 annual report).
details.funding_verdict: State Library of Queensland: state-funded statutory body with philanthropic support
funding: Total income was $101.823 million in 2025-26 ($101.620 million in 2024-25), of which grants and contributions were $93.724 million (2025-26 annual report).

Cash income comprised an administered grant of $77.083 million, other grants of $4.432 million, user charges of $6.046 million, donations and sponsorships of $1.499 million and interest of $1.250 million (2025-26 annual report).
A $9 million Queensland Government investment over 2023-26 funded the Digital Inclusion Program in regional and remote Queensland (2025-26 annual report).

Queensland Library Foundation established a corporate partnership with Personalised Plates Queensland as major sponsor of the 2025-26 summer exhibition Driven: every car has a story (2025-26 annual report).

Queensland Literary Awards supporters named for 2025-26 are The University of Queensland, University of Queensland Press, Copyright Agency's Cultural Fund, The Courier-Mail, Jenny Summerson, Susan Hocking and Ian Mackie and family, and the Talbot Foundation (2025-26 annual report).
Named donors include Gina and Tim Fairfax, the Ash Barty Foundation, Keith and Caroline Hamilton, The Siganto Foundation, Ken MacDonald and Terry White (2025-26 annual report).

Arrow Energy partnered with the State Library and Western Downs Libraries from December 2013 on the Creative Community Computing and Dads Read programs, as part of its Brighter Futures community investment (Arrow Energy, 5 December 2013).

red_flags.heading: Fossil fuel sponsorship
points: The ministerial diary records the Arts Minister, Ian Walker, speaking at the State Library/Arrow Energy Partnership launch with representatives of Arrow Energy and the State Library on 4 December 2013 (Queensland Government ministerial diary, December 2013).

Arrow described the partnership as part of more than $4 million it invested in communities that year, and the first Western Downs Dads Read day was held in Dalby on 8 March 2014 (Arrow Energy, 5 December 2013 and 5 March 2014).
Shell and PetroChina acquired Arrow Energy, a coal seam gas and LNG company, through a 50:50 joint venture cleared by the ACCC on 13 April 2010 (ACCC).

wider_context: Arrow Energy is not named among supporters in the 2024-25 or 2025-26 annual reports (State Library annual reports).
In 2025 the library rescinded a black&write! Writing Fellowship awarded to K. A. Ren Wyld after the Arts Minister instructed it to, and several Queensland Literary Awards judges resigned (Wikipedia).

case_notes.title: Queensland ministerial diary
case_notes.text: The Queensland ministerial diary records the Arts Minister, Ian Walker, speaking at the launch of the State Library's partnership with Arrow Energy, Shell's joint venture with PetroChina, before its representatives and guests on 4 December 2013.

grade_basis: A funder tied to fossil fuels.

name: Cadogan Hall
funding: Private company owned by Cadogan Estates. Turnover was £3.96M in 2025 and £3.82M in 2024, when it also booked £1M other operating income (2025 accounts).
watch: BP sponsored Mariinsky Orchestra concerts at the hall, including one on 18 April 2016 to which BP Russia invited the Culture Secretary.
why_flagged: BP Russia invited the Culture Secretary, John Whittingdale, to a BP-sponsored Mariinsky Orchestra performance of Romeo and Juliet at the hall on 18 April 2016, with the Russian Ambassador present (Art Not Oil, May 2016), and BP or not BP? protested at that concert (Slipped Disc, 19 April 2016).

overview: Built as a Church of Christ, Scientist, completed in 1907 to designs by Robert Fellowes Chisholm; the building was Grade II listed in April 1969 (Wikipedia).
Cadogan Estates Ltd, the property company of Earl Cadogan, bought the building in 2000, and Paul Davis and Partners refurbished it as a concert hall in 2004 at a cost of £7.5 million (Wikipedia).
The Royal Philharmonic Orchestra gave its first concert there in November 2004 and is resident at the hall, with Music Director Vasily Petrenko (Wikipedia; hall website).
The hall gives its capacity as 950 seats; Wikipedia gives 953 (hall website; Wikipedia).
The BBC staged a handful of Proms concerts there from 2005 to 2021 (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: Cadogan Hall: ticket and hire income at a venue owned by the Cadogan estate
funding: The hall is run by Cadogan Hall Limited, company 05036968, incorporated on 6 February 2004, whose principal activity is the management and operation of a concert hall venue (Companies House; 2025 accounts).

Turnover was £3,964,237 in 2025 and £3,819,078 in 2024; after cost of sales of £1,855,033 and administrative expenses of £2,114,147, it made a loss of £4,935 in 2025, against a profit of £740,813 in 2024 (2025 accounts).
The 2024 figures include other operating income of £1,000,000, with none in 2025; the accounts do not say where it came from (2025 accounts).

Its immediate parent is Cadogan Estates Limited and its operational holding company Cadogan Group Limited; ultimate ownership is vested in The Eighth Earl Cadogan's 6 December 1961 Settlement, and The Earl Cadogan is a director (2025 accounts).
The company employed an average of 16 people in 2025, with staff costs of £887,650 (2025 accounts).
The Zurich International Orchestra Series at the hall was sponsored by Zurich in the 2019-20 season (hall website).

red_flags.heading: Fossil fuel sponsorship of concerts at the hall
points: A Freedom of Information response reported by Art Not Oil confirmed that BP invited the Culture Secretary to a BP-sponsored performance of Romeo and Juliet conducted by Valery Gergiev at Cadogan Hall on 18 April 2016; the Russian Ambassador was also in attendance and Peter Charrow, Vice-President of BP Russia, made the invitation (Art Not Oil, BP's cultural sponsorship: A corrupting influence, May 2016).
Culture Unstained reports that BP committed to a 7-year sponsorship of the Mariinsky's UK tours, with performances at venues such as Cadogan Hall (Culture Unstained, Crude Connections).

red_flags.heading: Protest or boycott
points: Three performers from BP or not BP? protested on 18 April 2016 at the BP-sponsored Mariinsky Orchestra concert of Prokofiev's Romeo and Juliet at Cadogan Hall, against the sponsorship and Russian government policy (Slipped Disc, 19 April 2016).

wider_context: Culture Unstained describes Gergiev as a close friend and ally of Vladimir Putin and quotes him in a BP promotional video saying the sponsorship is bigger than sponsorship (Culture Unstained, Crude Connections).

case_notes.title: Art Not Oil Coalition, FOI releases
case_notes.text: Peter Charrow, vice-president of BP Russia, invited the Culture Secretary to a BP-sponsored performance of Romeo and Juliet conducted by Valery Gergiev at Cadogan Hall on 18 April 2016, with the Russian Ambassador also in attendance, according to freedom of information releases to the Art Not Oil Coalition.

grade_basis: A funder tied to fossil fuels. The record also holds a public protest.

name: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
funding: Nonprofit on Chicago Park District land. Of $70.2M revenue in 2025, $18.1M was admissions, $19.7M private support and $4.5M government support (audited financial statements).
watch: Nicor Gas, a natural gas distributor, is a contributing donor to the Powering the Future energy exhibit, which opened on 8 May 2026.
why_flagged: The museum names Nicor Gas, which distributes natural gas across northern Illinois (Wikipedia), as a contributing donor to its Powering the Future exhibit opening 8 May 2026 (museum press release, 2026).

overview: Founded by Julius Rosenwald, president of Sears, Roebuck and Company, the museum occupies the Palace of Fine Arts built for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, designed by Charles B. Atwood (Wikipedia).
It opened in 1933 during the Century of Progress Exposition, in stages between 1933 and 1940, in Jackson Park at 5700 South DuSable Lake Shore Drive (Wikipedia).

Legal title to the land and original building is vested with the Chicago Park District, and the museum holds the right to use and occupy them in perpetuity while it uses them for its incorporated purposes (2025 audited financial statements).
The museum reports over 1.5 million guests a year; its exhibits include the U-505 submarine, the Coal Mine, open since 1933, and the Henry Crown Space Center (2025 audited financial statements).
Chevy Humphrey has been president and CEO since January 2021 (Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: Griffin Museum of Science and Industry: admissions, a $125M founder-naming gift and Park District support, with energy company exhibit donors
funding: Total revenue and support was $70,248,070 in 2025: admissions $18,091,028, special exhibits $4,764,035, ancillary services $9,107,348, membership $4,063,896, government support $4,456,654, private support $19,654,060 and investment return designated for operations $6,300,010; net assets were $422,158,897 at year end (2025 audited financial statements).

Government support includes Chicago Park District funding based on the Park District's annual tax levy ordinance, and funding from federal and state agencies for research, programming and capital projects (2025 audited financial statements).

The 2024 Form 990 reports total revenue of $66,431,592, including contributions of $23,562,202, program service revenue of $21,993,865 and investment income of $6,957,912 (IRS Form 990 via ProPublica).

Kenneth C. Griffin, founder and CEO of Citadel, gave $125 million, announced in October 2019 and the largest gift in the museum's history; the museum took his name on 19 May 2024 (museum press release, May 2024).

Powering the Future is made possible by lead donor Exelon Foundation, contributing donors Nicor Gas and Invenergy, and donors including CDW, Ecolab, JL Family Foundation, Argonne National Laboratory, NOAA and Hubbell Utility Solutions (museum press release, 2026).
Bank of America sponsors three consecutive exhibitions, 007 Science, Marvel's Spider-Man: Beyond Amazing and Anne Frank The Exhibition, which opened on 1 May 2026 (museum press release).
Julius Rosenwald pledged $3 million toward converting the building and eventually gave more than $5 million (Wikipedia).

red_flags.heading: Fossil fuel donor to an energy exhibit
points: Nicor Gas, owned by Southern Company, distributes natural gas to more than two million customers in northern Illinois (Wikipedia), and is a contributing donor to the permanent Powering the Future exhibit, which the museum presents in tandem with its Coal Mine exhibit (museum press release, 2026).

wider_context: Illinois State Senator Robert Peters said on 14 May 2024 that the renaming "is demeaning to the core identity of MSI", and historian Shermann "Dilla" Thomas called it "a sting and a blow to Chicago and Chicago history" (Peters press release; ABC7, 14 May 2024).

The City of Chicago lobbying register lists the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry as a client of lobbyist Emily D. Ramsey in quarterly filings from July 2024 to September 2026, consulting on historic permit review issues with the Department of Planning and Development (City of Chicago lobbying data).

grade_basis: A funder tied to fossil fuels.

name: Meridian Hall
funding: City-owned, run by TO Live, a city board and charity. Of C$39.5M revenue in 2025, C$6.1M was City investment; Meridian Credit Union pays for naming rights (financial statements).

overview: Opened on 1 October 1960 as the O'Keefe Centre for the Performing Arts, paid for by the O'Keefe Brewery, to designs by Earle C. Morgan and Peter Dickinson; it seats 3,191 at 1 Front Street East (Wikipedia).
It was the home of the Canadian Opera Company and the National Ballet of Canada until 2006 (Wikipedia).

Named the Hummingbird Centre from February 1996 and the Sony Centre for the Performing Arts from 2007, it closed on 26 June 2008 for renovations and reopened on 1 October 2010; it took the name Meridian Hall on 15 September 2019 (Wikipedia).
The L Tower, a condominium designed by Daniel Libeskind and approved in 2006, stands on the southwest corner of the property (Wikipedia).

TO Live is a city board under the City of Toronto Act, 2006, operating Meridian Hall, the St. Lawrence Centre for the Arts and Meridian Arts Centre on behalf of the City, which owns them (TO Live 2025 financial statements).
details.funding_verdict: Meridian Hall: rentals, tickets, City funding and a credit union naming deal
funding: TO Live's revenue was C$39.54 million in 2025: rental C$15.59 million, ancillary C$8.45 million, performance C$4.15 million, City of Toronto investment C$6.148 million (C$5.599 million in 2024), and transfers including C$1.44 million from the State of Good Repair Program and C$300,000 from the Toronto Live Foundation (TO Live 2025 draft financial statements).
The City is responsible for TO Live's operating deficit and entitled to its surplus, and provides an operating line of credit of up to C$1.25 million (TO Live 2025 draft financial statements).

Proceeds from the name-in-title sponsor of C$1.945 million in 2025 (C$1.925 million in 2024) went to the Facility Fee Reserve Fund, alongside C$1.239 million from the ticket capital surcharge (TO Live 2025 draft financial statements).
The City of Toronto announced a C$30.75 million, fifteen-year naming partnership with Meridian Credit Union on 21 January 2019 (Wikipedia).
Sony bought the naming rights for C$10 million in September 2007 for a ten-year partnership, and Hummingbird Communications Ltd. gave C$5 million in 1996 (Wikipedia).
The Toronto Live Foundation received C$239,000 in donations in 2025 (C$2.47 million in 2024) and held fund balances of C$4.918 million at year end (TO Live 2025 draft financial statements).

TO Live prepares a semi-annual impact report for Meridian; the Q3 and Q4 2024 report says the partnership launched a new Indigenous arts festival (TO Live board report and Meridian sponsorship report, February 2025).

case_notes.title: Registry of Lobbyists (Canada)
case_notes.text: The board of the hall, then the Sony Centre for the Performing Arts, registered to lobby the federal government in 2008 and 2009 to obtain funding from Transport and Infrastructure Canada for its redevelopment plan, and reported communications with officials on economic development.

grade_basis: No flagged funder or funding protest on record, and the amounts are given.
